nameStory: This sage earned its "anise-scented" name from the sweet licorice-like fragrance released when you crush its leaves between your fingers. The alternative name "hummingbird sage" tells another story - those deep blue tubular flowers are perfectly designed to attract ruby-throated hummingbirds with their rich nectar.
description: Anise-scented sage is a tender perennial herb that forms bushy clumps 3-5 feet tall and wide. This South American native produces spikes of deep cobalt-blue tubular flowers that seem to glow against the backdrop of soft green, heart-shaped leaves. In New England, it's typically grown as an annual since it can't survive our winters, making appearances in gardens from summer through the first frost.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Deep cobalt or royal blue tubular flowers about 2 inches long, arranged in loose spikes. The flowers have a hooded upper lip and project forward from purple-tinged calyxes (the green cup that holds the petals).

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped to oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along square stems. Crush a leaf and you'll immediately smell the sweet anise or licorice fragrance that gives this plant its name.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, bushy clumps 3-5 feet tall with multiple branching stems. The plant has a soft, herbaceous texture and tends to spread outward as much as upward.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that feel slightly fuzzy to the touch - a classic trait of the mint family. The stems are green but may show purple tinting, especially near the flower clusters.

habitat: In New England, you'll find anise-scented sage exclusively in cultivated settings like flower gardens, containers, and landscaped areas. It thrives in rich, well-drained soil with full sun to partial shade and regular watering. Since it's not cold-hardy here, it's treated as an annual and won't survive outdoors through winter.

seasonality.spring: Young plants appear in garden centers and may be planted after the last frost. Early growth shows the characteristic heart-shaped leaves and square stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant deep blue flower spikes that attract hummingbirds and butterflies. The anise scent is strongest during warm weather.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming until the first hard frost kills the plant. Seeds may form in warmer autumns, appearing as small nutlets in the spent flower calyxes.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely and don't return - only survives as seed or if brought indoors as a houseplant in New England's climate.

funFact: The flowers are so perfectly designed for hummingbird pollination that the birds' heads fit exactly into the tubular blooms, ensuring they get dusted with pollen while sipping nectar - this co-evolution happened over millions of years in South America, yet it works just as well with our North American ruby-throated hummingbirds!
confusionNotes: The deep blue tubular flowers might remind you of other hummingbird plants like bee balm, but crushing the leaves instantly reveals the diagnostic sweet licorice scent that no other common garden plant shares.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "sage," this plant is quite different from the gray-leaved culinary sage used in cooking. Both are in the same genus (Salvia) but have very different appearances, scents, and uses - anise-scented sage is purely ornamental and not used for seasoning.
compareHints: Unlike the native lyreleaf sage with its small purple flowers and basal rosette of leaves, anise-scented sage forms tall bushy plants with much larger, intensely blue flowers. Most other Salvia species in our region have smaller flowers and lack the distinctive sweet anise fragrance when the leaves are crushed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike lyreleaf sage which has distinctive lobed basal leaves and prefers shady woods, giant blue sage has narrow, unlobed leaves and demands full sun.
Unlike other sages that might be found in New England gardens like lyreleaf sage (which has much broader, lobed leaves), mintweed has very narrow, simple leaves and a weedy appearance.
Unlike native New England sages like lyreleaf sage, chia is much taller and more robust, growing 3-5 feet compared to the 1-2 foot height of most regional relatives.
Unlike our native Lyreleaf Sage which has deeply lobed leaves and purple flowers, Sticky Sage has simple heart-shaped leaves and yellow flowers.
Lyreleaf sage is the only Salvia species you're likely to encounter in New England, making it unique in the region.
